summary:
Venezuela presents a mixed and unstable picture for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised, and the country has produced visible trans political figures, but there is no legal gender recognition procedure, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. Trans people therefore have no route to amend identity documents, and conduct targeting them carries no dedicated legal penalty.

The European Union Asylum Agency maintains a dedicated LGBTIQ+ country profile for Venezuela as part of its reference material for international protection decisions, and the AFS Vance Center published an LGBTQ guide covering Venezuela in October 2024. The existence of these dedicated reference documents reflects a shared assessment among international bodies that LGBTIQ+ people in the country face conditions serious enough to underpin protection claims, even though the underlying conduct is not formally criminalised.

Since the disputed presidential election of July 2024, LGBTQ Venezuelans have faced persecution documented by rights observers as unprecedented, tied directly to the political crisis; the opposition presidential candidate left the country on 7 September 2024. The persecution is not framed as gender-based in isolation, but the broader repression wave has swept in LGBTQ people, and arbitrary detention powers are applied broadly against perceived dissidents.

State targeting of LGBT politicians is documented. In December 2015, Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla, a Voluntad Popular deputy and the country's first openly gay parliamentarian, a prisoner of conscience held in the custody of the national intelligence service, SEBIN. He marked his 33rd birthday in his cell. That case establishes that openly LGBT political participation can attract direct state retaliation rather than institutional protection.

Trans political participation has nonetheless had precedents. In August 2015, Tamara Adán became Venezuela's first transgender candidate for the National Assembly. Her candidacy was possible because candidacy rules did not require the document amendments that trans people cannot obtain in the absence of a legal gender recognition process; the visibility did not translate into a recognition framework.

On marriage and partnership, the record shows a legislative push without enactment. In January 2014 an equal-marriage bill was reported as set to be presented to the National Assembly within the week, and no later enactment of that measure is recorded in the sources.

Public opinion data points in a comparatively supportive direction. A poll conducted in early March 2023 found that a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ+ population should hold the same rights as other citizens; 82% recognised the term LGBTIQ+, and 36% considered gay, lesbian and bisexual orientation to be innate. Societal tolerance, where documented, is not matched by any statutory protection.

For a trans visitor, the practical risk is less a matter of targeted gender-based enforcement than of a collapsed institutional environment: no anti-discrimination remedy, no hate-crime mechanism, degraded healthcare including access to hormone therapy, and predatory policing that applies to everyone regardless of identity. There is no institutional recourse when things go wrong.
tangentialFactors:
The legal environment must be read against the political crisis rather than against a trans-specific statute, since the persecution documented after July 2024 operates through general powers of detention and intimidation applied to perceived dissidents. LGBTQ people are affected as part of that wave rather than through a named LGBTIQ+ offence.

The 2023 polling data shows that documented public attitudes are more supportive than the legal framework would suggest. A majority backed equal rights for the LGBTIQ+ population, and familiarity with the term was high at 82%. The gap between that recorded opinion and the absence of any anti-discrimination or gender-recognition law is a point of contrast for anyone comparing Venezuela with neighbouring jurisdictions.

The record contains no evidence that Venezuela follows the regional trend toward same-sex marriage legislation. The 2014 equal-marriage bill is the only legislative milestone noted, and no enactment follows it in the sources, which is consistent with the country's broader pattern of stalled rights legislation during the period of economic and political crisis.

The AFS Vance Center LGBTQ guide of October 2024 and the EUAA country profile are comparative reference points rather than evidence of conditions in their own right. They indicate how international practitioners assess the country, and they are the kind of documentation a visitor could consult alongside their own planning.
localsOnly:
Resident trans people have no legal route to obtain gender recognition, which means identity documents remain mismatched for the duration of a person's life unless they leave the country or find a foreign procedure that applies. The same absence affects marriage, employment formalities, and any interaction requiring a consistent legal identity.

No anti-discrimination statute protects gender identity in employment, housing, healthcare or public services, and there is no hate-crime legislation against which targeted violence could be prosecuted as a distinct offence. Recourse, where it exists at all, runs through general criminal law with all of its evidentiary and institutional weaknesses.

Openly LGBT political activity has produced documented state retaliation. The case of Rosmit Mantilla, imprisoned under SEBIN custody after being declared a prisoner of conscience by Amnesty International, shows that visibility in public life can lead to detention rather than to any form of official protection.

Healthcare access has deteriorated to the point where hormone therapy and other trans-specific care are unreliable, and the collapse of public services removes the possibility of complaining about denial of care through any functioning channel. Trans women have historically been visible in urban life, but that visibility coexists with policing that is predatory toward the population at large and with no institutional mechanism for redress.
outOfScopeNotes:
The contents of the AFS Vance Center guide and of the EUAA LGBTIQ+ country profile are cited here only as reference documents; their specific findings on risk factors, safe regions, or protective actors are not detailed in the available inventory and remain unresolved.

Whether any sub-national authority in Venezuela has adopted anti-discrimination or gender-recognition measures of its own is not addressed by the sources. The national absence of such laws is established; the local position is not.

The outcome of Tamara Adán's 2015 candidacy, and whether she or any later trans candidate subsequently won office, is not sourced here. Only the candidacy itself is documented.

The legal procedure, if any, by which a resident could obtain a foreign gender recognition or rely on consular action from another country is not addressed in the sources and is treated as unresolved.

The exact legal basis on which SEBIN held Rosmit Mantilla, and whether his case remained active after December 2015, are not covered by the inventory.
